Feudal is an adjective. It means: relating to, or characteristic of, feudalism — a specific way of organizing society, power, land, and people that was common in medieval Europe (roughly from the 9th to the 15th century).

When you call something "feudal," you are saying it belongs to, resembles, or comes from that system.
To Understand "Feudal," You Must Understand Feudalism

You cannot truly understand the word "feudal" without understanding the system it describes. Think of it like the word "democratic" — it only makes full sense once you understand democracy.

Feudalism was a pyramid of power built on land and loyalty.

Here is how it worked:

Imagine a triangle. At the very top sat the king. He owned — at least in theory — all the land in the kingdom. But he could not manage all of it himself. So he divided large portions of his land (these portions were called fiefs) and gave them to powerful men — lords, barons, and nobles. In return, these men swore an oath of loyalty to the king and promised to provide him with soldiers and military support when needed.

These lords then did the same thing one level down. They took their land and divided portions of it to give to knights. The knights, in return, swore loyalty to their lord and promised to fight for him.

At the very bottom of this triangle sat the largest group: the peasants and serfs. They did not own land. They lived on the lord's land, farmed it, and gave the lord a portion of whatever they grew. In exchange, the lord gave them protection — from invaders, criminals, and rival lords.

So the entire system was a chain of land given in exchange for loyalty and service. Every person owed something to the person above them.

When you use the word "feudal," it almost always points to one or more of these core features:

1. A rigid social hierarchy
Everyone had a fixed place. You were born a serf, and you died a serf. There was very little movement between levels.

2. Land as the source of all power
In a feudal society, land was wealth. Whoever controlled the land controlled everything — food, people, armies.

3. Personal loyalty and obligation
Relationships in feudal society were built on sworn oaths. Your lord protected you; you served your lord. This personal bond — rather than laws or rights — held the society together.

4. Decentralized power
Power was not concentrated in one government. Instead, it was spread across many lords, each ruling their own territory almost like mini-kings.

In historical contexts:

This is the most direct use. When talking about medieval history, "feudal" simply describes things that belonged to or came out of this system.

  • "The feudal system organized European society for centuries."
  • "Under feudal law, the peasant had almost no rights."
  • "A feudal lord could demand taxes and labor from the people on his land."
  • "Feudal society was built on strict divisions between classes."
  • "The knight pledged his sword in a feudal ceremony of loyalty."

In modern or metaphorical contexts:

This is where "feudal" gets a second life. Today, people sometimes use "feudal" to describe modern situations that remind them of the old feudal system — especially when something feels outdated, oppressive, or unfairly hierarchical.

  • "The working conditions in that factory were practically feudal — workers had no rights and no voice."
  • "Some critics called the landlord's control over the village feudal."
  • "He ran his company in a feudal way — everyone had to go through him for everything."

In this metaphorical sense, calling something "feudal" is almost always a criticism. It implies the thing is archaic (old-fashioned), unfair, and based on blind obedience to authority rather than justice or equality.
The Emotional and Critical Weight of the Word

"Feudal" is not a neutral word when used in modern conversation. When someone today describes something as feudal, they are usually expressing disapproval. The word carries the suggestion that:

  • Power is in the hands of a very few
  • Ordinary people are treated as tools or property rather than as individuals with rights
  • The system is from an era humanity has moved past (or should have)
  • Loyalty is demanded rather than earned

It helps to know what the word does not mean:

  • It does not simply mean "old" or "ancient." Ancient Rome was old, but it was not feudal.
  • It does not mean "violent" or "warlike" on its own, even though feudal society had plenty of warfare.
  • It does not just mean "unfair" in a vague sense — it refers specifically to that kind of unfairness: one rooted in a hierarchy of land, class, and personal obligation.

What it describesAnything relating to the system of feudalism
That system's core ideaLand and power flow downward in exchange for loyalty and service flowing upward
In historical useDirectly describes medieval society, laws, relationships, and structures
In modern useA critical label for something that feels oppressively old-fashioned, hierarchical, or unjust
The feeling it carriesOften disapproval — suggesting something belongs to a less enlightened age

In short: feudal describes a world where your entire life — your safety, your home, your food, your social position — depended on who was above you in a rigid chain of power, and where you owed that person everything in return. When you call something feudal today, you are saying it still works that way, and that is not a compliment.
